summary:
I've been running a single GPU across five or six different model backends — a chat model, an image generator, a coding assistant's local brain, a roleplay model — instead of buying more hardware. The interesting part was making requests queue instead of stepping on each other: when one backend is already warm and holding memory, I skip the reload entirely rather than evicting and reloading it every single time. That one change took a routine request from 16 seconds down to about 5.

On a D&D campaign manager I built (TheLongRest), I found a bug where the combat tracker stored "whose turn it is" as a position in a list instead of a reference to the actual creature. So if you edited someone's initiative mid-fight, or a monster died and got removed, the turn indicator would silently jump to the wrong combatant — nobody skipped visibly, but the DM would suddenly be resolving the wrong creature's turn. Fixed it by tracking the active combatant by ID and deriving the turn order from that, then wrote a regression test that reproduces the exact scenario (edit initiative, delete above the active slot, delete the last active one) so it can't quietly regress.

I also moved that app's video calling from a per-table "bring your own API keys" setup to a single hosted backend, gated behind subscription tiers. Two bugs only showed up once it hit production: the video library worked fine in local dev but the production build (which uses a different bundler) silently stripped it out of the browser bundle, and separately the content-security-policy blocked the connection because nobody had updated it for the new video host. Both were the kind of thing that passes every local test and only breaks once real users hit the deployed site — good reminder to actually load the built artifact, not just trust the dev server.

Rounding it out, BudgetTracker — a personal finance tracker I built and run for myself — is live and now exposes its data through a small set of read-only API tools so an assistant can pull real numbers (account balances, spending trends) instead of guessing. Wiring that up surfaced a few database bugs around date handling that only showed up when the queries got hit with parameters instead of hardcoded test values, which is usually where that class of bug hides.

highlights.oneLiner: One GPU serving 5-6 model backends; warm-backend skip cut a request from 16s to 5s
Live personal finance tracker now exposes read-only API tools for real account/spending data
